newsitem.title: CANADA: Arakis may be vulnerable to takeover -CEO.
newsitem.headline: Arakis may be vulnerable to takeover -CEO.

text.p: Arakis Energy Corp, which recently concluded a deal to develop its oil concession in Sudan, may be vulnerable to a takeover attempt and is developing a plan to protect its shareholders, its chief executive, John McLeod, said on Friday.
Speculation of a possible suitor for Calgary-based Arakis intensified recently as the signed agreements made the company's future and the potential of its oil project appear more secure.

"We don't have a major shareholder and look at the volume of our stock -- somebody could probably pick it up if they got after it," McLeod said in a telephone interview from Victoria, British Columbia.
"We're working on a shareholder protection plan as well. There should be an announcement out very shortly on some of these things," he said.

Earlier this month, Arakis and its three partners in the 12.2-million-acre concession in the south of strife-torn Sudan signed final agreements for the project's development and the building of a 950-mile oil pipeline to the Red Sea.

Partners under the agreement include Arakis with 25 percent, China National Petroleum Corp with 40 percent, Malaysia state oil company Petronas with 30 percent and the Sudan government with 5 percent.
The potential reserves of the concession may range as high as 3.5 billion barrels of oil, according to some estimates. Arakis has said it is comfortable with a 600 million barrel figure.

The company is expected to release results early next week from three prospects -- the El Nar, El Toor and Toma South wells. Results are also expected in the coming weeks from the closely watched Umm Sagura prospect. Analysts said the test results could mean a large boost in reserve estimates.

Still, Arakis's stock has languished at less than US$4 a share for months, climbing higher than that level only this week. Arakis closed down 6/16 on Friday to 4-7/16 on Nasdaq volume of 3.4 million shares.
McLeod said a shareholder plan would be structured mostly to increase the time afforded the company's board to pursue options if a bid were launched.
"I'm not interested in entrenching management or anything like that. I just want to make sure that if anything like this happens, the shareholders get a fair deal," he said.
Bill Magee, an analyst with Credifinance Securities in Toronto, said the takeover speculation was not new, but it has recently picked up among those who follow the company.

"It has been around as an obvious thing that could happen for a long time because the stock is very widely held, there's no control block and management doesn't control a lot," Magee said. Credifinance is sponsoring Arakis in its application to list its shares on the Toronto Stock Exchange.
He said he pegged Arakis's present value at about US$6 per share, based on reserve estimates from last year.

Based on Arakis's closing price on Friday and its 93 million fully diluted shares, its market capitalization would total US$407 million. It has some cash as a result of monthly payments from its project partners and no long-term debt.

Some potential suitors mentioned by analysts and others who closely follow the company include Vancouver-based International Petroleum Corp (IPC), which recently picked up an exploration block adjacent to the Arakis group's lands in Sudan. Also mentioned are Petronas, which is involved on both concessions, and Occidental Petroleum Corp.

Occidental was involved in negotiations to gain interests in the Arakis and IPC projects, but it did not conclude a deal in either. Its potential involvement in Sudan became controversial in view of U.S. anti-terrorism legislation.
